newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fur engulfs Paris couture club.
newsitem.headline: Fur engulfs Paris couture club.

text.p: The man who once swore he used only recycled or fake fur closed ranks with the rest of the Paris couture club on Wednesday and sent out hides belonging to creatures ranging from monkey to mink.

Jean-Paul Gaultier, in his second stab at haute couture, unleashed fox head stoles over pinstripe trouser suits, foamy Mongolian lamb hats and a kimono and bridal gown of breitschwarntz, the velvety fur of baby astrakhans supposedly born dead, a hit on several catwalks this season.

The secret to this season's fur craze is that the fur industry, devastated by political correctness, has given the couture houses animal skins for free, hoping the thousands of pages of magazine photographs will help revive the market.
Gaultier as usual had a gimmick, and here it was the babushka, all braids and head shawls that were trotted out accompanied by musicians playing gypsy tunes.
There were also aubergine satin suits brocaded with velvet flowers, oversized satin snowsuits covered with black tulle and enormous leg of lamb sleeves on taffeta gowns.

It was half serious couture ands half fun, as with huge coats of monkey hair or ostrich feathers, a male model in a sequin embroidered sheepskin coat or a dress of black lace, spiralled from shoulders to toes with pink shawl fringe.
The real clothes were beautiful bustier gowns of bordeaux or bruised plum velvet, a tuxedo dress with puffed sleeves and a peach satin lining, and a black crepe jumpsuit.
"It was definitely, completely extravagant," said ready-to-wear designer Sonia Rykiel. "There were stunning, beautiful, magic things, and then the funny side of it, with fantastic workmanship."
Yves Saint Laurent looked to the old masters to inspire his Autumn/Winter haute couture collection on Wednesday, a sombre parade of gowns echoing the royal courts of the Renaissance.

Black velvet princess gowns, their waists elongated, and rounded necklines edged with rich sable, recalled the shadowed works of Clouet, court painter to France's Valois dynasty, Flemish artist Frans Hals and the mistresses of French kings.
Gold crosses dangled from models' necks and feathers shivered atop Shakespearean caps.
The flowers of a mediaeval tapestry trickled down pinegreen velvet sleeves and period gems and gilt filigree glistened from the collar of a dark robe.
The embroidered, jewel-encrusted bolero made a comeback, as did Saint Laurent's signature black "smoking" evening suits, here with masculine tailoring and cummerbunds or simple and classically cut.
Fur, genuine fox, sable and mink, seemed to be everywhere, for indoors and out -- on hats, shawls, the cuffs of gloves and as trim on gowns or suits.

"I was inspired by the black in Clouet's portraits, the gowns of Diane de Poitiers, the portraits of the de Medicis. I thought of the darkness of Rembrandt ciseled with gold and sable and of the very pure elongated shape of the body," Saint Laurent told reporters.
"Nothing is left but the line of the body. Unfortunately it makes me suffer more and more because it's very difficult."
